title: PROVERBS 5 DOESN’T MERELY SAY “AVOID ADULTERY”—IT SAYS “ENJOY YOUR WIFE”
paragraphs: PROVERBS 5 DOESN’T MERELY SAY “AVOID ADULTERY”—IT SAYS “ENJOY YOUR WIFE”
God’s answer to forbidden desire is not merely a locked door. He points a husband back toward the woman he vowed to love—and says, “Rejoice.”
There is a devastating moment in Proverbs 5 that many people rush past.
Maybe because we already think we know what the chapter says.
Don’t commit adultery.
Don’t sleep with someone else’s wife.
Stay away from sexual temptation.
Be faithful.
All true.
But if that is all you hear when you read Proverbs 5, you have stopped reading before reaching one of the most startlingly beautiful things God says about marriage.
Because Scripture does not merely tell a husband what woman he must avoid.
It tells him what woman he should enjoy.
And that changes the entire conversation.

The father speaking to his son begins with a warning. Forbidden desire looks sweet before it becomes bitter. The temptation sounds smooth before the consequences begin screaming. What promises pleasure can eventually demand your honor, your years, your strength, your peace, your reputation, and your home.
Sin rarely introduces itself by showing you the funeral.
It shows you the flowers.
It doesn't show you the wife crying in the bedroom.
It shows you the message that made you feel wanted.
It doesn't show you the children wondering why Dad no longer lives at home.
It shows you the thrill.
It doesn't show you years of rebuilding trust.
It shows you ten minutes of secrecy.
It doesn't show you standing before God with everything exposed.
It whispers:
“No one will know.”
And then Proverbs says something terrifying:
God already does.
“For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD.”
Nothing is hidden.
Not the hotel room.
Not the deleted conversation.
Not the second account.
Not the flirtation you keep calling harmless.
Not the emotional relationship you insist “isn't technically cheating.”
Not the pornography nobody knows you watch.
Not the comparison silently poisoning the way you look at your spouse.
Not the fantasy you continue feeding while physically remaining faithful.
God sees the road long before everybody else sees the wreckage.
But Proverbs 5 is not merely God standing beside the highway shouting, “DON'T GO THERE!”
There is another road.
And this is where the chapter becomes breathtaking.
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.”
Then comes Proverbs 5:18:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha barukh, uśemaḥ me'eshet ne'urekha.
A faithful sense of the Hebrew is:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Look carefully at that word:
וּשְׂמַח — uśemaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
God could have stopped at prohibition.
He didn't.
He could simply have said, “Do not touch another woman.”
Instead, He turns the husband's eyes homeward.
Look at your wife.
The woman whose face you have seen tired.
The woman who has seen you without the polished version everyone else gets.
The woman who knows your strange habits, your weaknesses, your unfinished sentences, your fears, your failures.
The woman beside whom ordinary life happened.
Bills.
Children.
Laundry.
Arguments.
Sickness.
Work.
Disappointment.
Birthdays.
Funerals.
Morning breath.
Unanswered prayers.
Unexpected laughter.
Years.
And Scripture says:
Rejoice in her.
That matters because biblical faithfulness is much richer than merely avoiding another person's bed.
A marriage can contain no physical adultery and still become painfully empty.
You can remain legally married while becoming emotionally absent.
You can share an address while living separate lives.
You can sleep six inches apart and somehow feel six thousand miles away.
You can become experts at schedules, bills, children, responsibilities, groceries, church attendance, and getting through another week...
while forgetting how to delight in each other.
And perhaps one of the saddest sentences a spouse can silently carry is:
“I know you haven't left me.
But I don't know if you still want me.”
Proverbs 5 speaks directly into that distance.
The chapter's answer to adultery is not merely restraint.
It is redirected delight.
The text continues with startlingly physical language about the husband's wife, telling him to find satisfaction in her and remain captivated by her love.
God is not embarrassed by marital intimacy.
We often are.
God isn't.
We sometimes talk as though holiness means pretending married people aren't sexual creatures.
Scripture doesn't.
Sexual desire is not inherently dirty.
God created the covenant in which sexual intimacy belongs.

Genesis presents husband and wife becoming “one flesh.” Proverbs celebrates marital delight. Song of Songs speaks unabashedly of desire between lovers. The New Testament continues treating marriage as honorable and marital faithfulness as sacred.
The biblical answer to sexual chaos is therefore not hatred of sexuality.
It is holiness.
There is a difference.
Holiness doesn't say the fire is evil.
Holiness puts the fire in the fireplace so it warms the house instead of burning the house down.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that because perhaps you were taught only to fear desire.
Maybe sex was spoken about so shamefully that even after marriage you carried the shame into the marriage bed.
Maybe nobody taught you that tenderness between husband and wife could actually be received with gratitude before God.
Or perhaps your story is completely different.
Perhaps you crossed the line.
Maybe Proverbs 5 isn't theoretical for you.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you had the affair.
Maybe you became addicted to pornography.
Maybe you betrayed somebody who trusted you.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret that would change the atmosphere of your home if it were exposed.
Then don't misuse this article as an excuse to hide longer.
Sin grows remarkably well in darkness.
Jesus calls sinners into the light.
And this is where we must move from Proverbs to the heart of the Gospel.
Because Christianity's message is not:
Good people never fall.
Christianity's message is that sinners need a Savior.
David knew what sexual sin could destroy.
He took Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that resulted in Uriah's death. When Nathan confronted him, David could no longer hide behind royal power.
His response became one of Scripture's most painful prayers:
“Have mercy upon me, O God.”
That is where restoration begins.
Not with excuses.
Not with blaming your spouse.
Not with “I was lonely.”
Not with “She wasn't meeting my needs.”
Not with “He stopped paying attention to me.”
Not with “It was only online.”
Not with “Nothing physical happened.”
Repentance stops negotiating with the truth.
It confesses.
And then grace does something scandalous.
It meets the guilty person there.

This does not mean consequences disappear. Forgiveness does not make betrayal imaginary. Trust may require a long rebuilding process. Deep wounds do not close because someone says “sorry” once. In situations involving betrayal, abuse, coercion, or danger, simplistic advice about intimacy can cause further harm; wisdom, safety, truthful accountability, and qualified pastoral or professional help may be necessary.
But the Gospel announces something even our worst chapter cannot erase:
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
The ashamed.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer who repents.
The pornography addict who finally stops pretending.
The betrayed spouse trying to understand how to breathe again.
The husband realizing he spent years starving his marriage of affection.
The wife wondering whether she is still beautiful in her husband's eyes.
The single believer fighting desires nobody knows about.
The person whose past makes them wonder whether God could ever call them clean.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the edited version of us.
He died for sinners.
And resurrection means sin does not get the final sentence.
That is why our Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Not because Jesus calls evil good.
He doesn't.
Jesus rewrites everything because He confronts sin, bears judgment for sinners, offers forgiveness to those who come to Him, and begins transforming people who could never transform themselves.
Grace doesn't rename adultery.
Grace redeems adulterers.
Grace doesn't pretend betrayal didn't hurt.
Grace enters the wound.
Grace doesn't say repentance is unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine repentance possible.
And if you are married, perhaps Proverbs 5 is asking you a question more uncomfortable than, “Have you committed adultery?”
Perhaps it is asking:
Are you rejoicing in the spouse God has given you?
When was the last time you looked at your wife without comparing her to somebody filtered through a screen?
When was the last time you pursued her without wanting something in return?
When was the last time you touched her affectionately without every touch becoming a demand?
When was the last time you told her she was beautiful—and made her believe you meant it?
When did you last ask what she is afraid of?
What she dreams about?
What has been hurting?
What she needs prayer for?
When was the last time the two of you laughed until something inside the marriage felt young again?
Some men will spend enormous energy resisting temptation while spending almost no energy cultivating tenderness.
Proverbs points toward something better.
Don't merely run away from the strange woman.
Run home.
Don't merely delete the number.
Recover the conversation you stopped having with your wife.
Don't merely close the browser.
Open your heart.
Don't merely stop feeding fantasy.
Start feeding covenant love.
Don't merely ask God to make another woman less attractive.
Ask Him to teach you again how to cherish the woman beside you.
And wives should not hear this passage as though they carry responsibility for preventing their husbands' sin.
They don't.
A husband's adultery is not automatically evidence that his wife failed him. Scripture places moral responsibility on the person choosing sin.
Nor does Proverbs 5 teach that a wife exists merely for a husband's gratification.
Biblical marriage is covenantal, personal, loving, faithful, and ultimately shaped by the self-giving love revealed in Christ.
The New Testament makes the standard even more demanding.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Think about that.
Christ's model for husbands is not consumption.
It is sacrifice.
Not:
“What can she give me?”
But:
“How can I love her?”
Not entitlement.
Self-giving.
Not domination.
Service.
Not treating your wife's body as something owed to you.
Cherishing the whole person who entrusted her life to you.
This means Proverbs 5:19 cannot honestly be turned into biblical permission for selfishness or coercion.
Marital delight separated from marital love becomes another form of taking.
But Christ teaches husbands to give themselves.
And perhaps that is where somebody's marriage begins changing.
Not tonight in the bedroom.
But this afternoon in the kitchen.
With dishes.
With an apology.
With a phone being put down.
With eye contact.
With listening.
With forgiveness.
With:
“I haven't loved you the way Christ calls me to love you.”
Maybe romance begins again with repentance.
Maybe intimacy begins again with safety.
Maybe desire begins growing where tenderness has been replanted.
Maybe the miracle you keep asking God to perform in your marriage begins with something painfully ordinary:
You turn toward each other again.
Because the grass is not greener wherever temptation points.
Grass becomes greener where somebody faithfully waters it.
And Proverbs has been talking about water all along.
Your cistern.
Your well.
Your fountain.
Your covenant.
Your wife.
Your husband.
Your home.
Your marriage.
Water what God has entrusted to you.
The world will constantly offer alternatives.
A younger face.
A more attentive coworker.
An old flame who suddenly messages.
A stranger who laughs at your jokes.
A fantasy requiring none of the patience real marriage demands.
A screen offering bodies without covenant, pleasure without responsibility, and stimulation without sacrifice.
But fantasies never have to wake up with sick children.
Pornography never asks you to practice forgiveness.
An affair doesn't show you the mundane years that would eventually arrive there too.
Forbidden desire sells you a highlight reel while hiding the invoice.
Proverbs shows you the invoice.
Honor.
Years.
Strength.
Peace.
And ultimately the cords of sin itself.
But then wisdom points toward something temptation cannot manufacture:
Covenant.
To know someone...
and still choose them.
To age together.
To forgive.
To rediscover.
To endure seasons when feelings fluctuate.
To watch youthful attraction mature into something temptation cannot imitate because temptation has no history with you.
There is holiness in that.
There is beauty in wrinkles that arrived while two people kept choosing one another.
There is something profoundly sacred about hands that no longer look twenty-five holding each other after decades of storms.
“The wife of your youth” eventually becomes the wife of your old age.
And if God grants you those years, may you still look across the room and know:
There she is.
The woman I chose.
The woman I hurt sometimes.
The woman who forgave me.
The woman I forgave.
The woman with whom I built ordinary Tuesdays and unforgettable years.
My friend.
My covenant companion.
My beloved.
Rejoice.
Not because marriage is always easy.
Not because your spouse is perfect.
Not because attraction never requires cultivation.
Rejoice because covenant love is worth protecting.
And if your marriage is hurting right now, don't turn this article into another weapon.
Don't send it to your spouse with:
“SEE? YOU'RE THE PROBLEM.”
Read it first as a mirror.
Ask:
“Lord, what needs to change in me?”
Because transformation almost always becomes harder when we are obsessed with somebody else's repentance.
And for the person who isn't married, Proverbs 5 still speaks.
It tells you something about desire.
You do not become free by obeying every appetite.
Some desires must be denied because God loves you too much to call destruction freedom.
Jesus went even deeper than external adultery when He addressed lust arising in the heart.
So purity is not merely keeping bodies apart.
It reaches the imagination.
The eyes.
The heart.
The secret life.
That is why we need more than rules.
We need Christ.
We need new hearts.
We need the Holy Spirit producing what willpower alone cannot sustain.
We need grace when we fail and strength to walk differently afterward.
Maybe you have been hiding.
This could be the moment hiding ends.
Not because thousands of strangers on Facebook need your private details.
They don't.
But because Jesus is calling you out of darkness.
Talk to God truthfully.
Seek trustworthy, mature Christian accountability.
Where serious marital wounds exist, seek wise pastoral care and appropriate professional counseling.
Bring sin into the light instead of feeding it privately.
If necessary, take concrete steps that make obedience costly but possible.
And remember:
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
Be honest.
Sometimes the hardest person to stop deceiving is ourselves.
And if you know a husband who needs to remember that faithfulness is more than avoiding adultery, tag him—not to shame him, but because marriages are worth strengthening.
If you know a couple quietly fighting for their covenant, send this to them privately.
Not as a badge announcing that your marriage is perfect.
One share may put Scripture in front of someone before temptation gets the final word.

That is one simple way you can help spread biblical truth and glorify God—but supporting Gospel work should flow from willing worship and conviction, never guilt or the idea that God's favor can be purchased.
Invite your husband. Invite your wife. Invite your family. Invite the friend struggling secretly. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker who isn't sure what they believe yet.
But after all the Hebrew, all the warnings, all the discussion about marriage, sexuality, temptation, repentance, and restoration, don't miss the heart of this chapter.
God does not merely want you standing far away from adultery congratulating yourself because you never crossed the line.
He wants your heart.
He wants holiness reaching into your desires.
He wants covenant protected.
He wants husbands learning to cherish rather than consume.
He wants wives loved as people rather than treated as objects.
He wants wounded marriages brought into truth.
He wants secret sin dragged into light.
He wants sinners running toward Christ instead of hiding behind religious appearances.
And He wants us to discover that His commands are not arbitrary fences around human happiness.
Sometimes the fence is there because there is a cliff on the other side.
Proverbs 5 shows us both.
The cliff...
and the fountain.
One path says:
Take what isn't yours.
The other says:
Rejoice in what God has entrusted to you.
One promises sweetness and ends in bitterness.
The other requires covenant faithfulness and can deepen into a kind of love lust could never manufacture.
So husband...
go home.
Look at your wife.
Not through the eyes of pornography.
Not through the eyes of comparison.
Not through the resentment of your latest argument.
Ask God to help you see her again.
Remember the girl you once prayed would say yes.
Remember the vows.
Remember the years.
Remember the mercy God has shown both of you.
And then love the woman standing in front of you now.
Not merely the memory of who she was.
Her.
Now.
And if your story already contains scandal...
remember this:
Peter's failure wasn't his final chapter.
David's sin wasn't the final sentence over his life.
The woman caught in adultery encountered Someone greater than the crowd holding stones.
The cross itself looked like history's darkest scandal until the empty tomb revealed that God was writing redemption through it.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds are real.
Your consequences may be painful.
But Jesus Christ is still Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive grace.
Walk differently.
Love faithfully.
And when temptation whispers that forbidden water will finally satisfy your thirst, remember the fountain God told you to bless.
Because sometimes the marriage Satan wants you to abandon is the very place where Christ is teaching you how covenant love survives the fire.
